subject: On using multivariate priors for non-varying parameters

messages.author: 29ce8550baceaeb0
messages.subject: On using multivariate priors for non-varying parameters
parts:
Hi all, 

A conceptual question: how should I think about using multivariate priors for parameters that do not vary (across groups, time periods, etc)? For example, in a linear regression y = XB + e, giving a multi-normal prior to B. At school I was taught to use multivariate priors, and in many papers I see it done. But a) I've run some experiments with known parameters, for simple models, and using multivariate priors doesn't appear to improve inference. And b) I have difficulty seeing why someone would use a multivariate distribution when there is only one group. The posterior summarizes covariance between my parameters even if my priors don't have any explicit covariance. 

Would appreciate any thoughts.

Jim

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] On using multivariate priors for non-varying parameters
parts:
If you have a vector of parameters b, you’d put a correlated prior on b if this reflects your uncertainty about the parameter.  What I will usually like to do is transform the elements of b so that I am comfortable with independent priors on the transformed space.  For example, suppose the X’s are 5 different economic indicators.  Then you might want to parameterize b_k = a*gamma_k, for k=1,…,5, where a is some shared scale parameter that gets a prior, and gamma_1,…,gamma_5 have independent priors.

Even more than that, I’d like to put X_1,…X_5 on a common scale so that gamma_1,…,gamma_5 can have priors that are identically distributed as well as being independent.

A

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] On using multivariate priors for non-varying parameters
parts:
My _guess_ is that multivariate priors were a response to not standardizing
the continuous covariates in the design matrix.  For example, if you include
both x_{1} = chi and x_{2} = chi^{2} and chi is entirely positive or negative
then we know a priori that beta_{1} and beta_{2} will be strongly correlated,
and that a priori knowledge can be incorporated into a multivariate prior.
As Andrew notes, once the covariates have been standardized then an IID
prior is much more natural.  

These is one of the reasons why reading economics papers makes me sad.  :-p

messages.author: 29ce8550baceaeb0
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] On using multivariate priors for non-varying parameters
parts:
Wasn't Andrew making the point the other week that if we scale covariates and then select a prior, 
the prior is actually conceived with knowledge of the data, and isn't really a prior? This is a part of 
my confusion. In any case, I think Andrew's point above is about scaling the parameters, not the 
covariates. 

What would make sense to me is if using a multivariate prior helped old-school samplers better
explore the parameter space. 

In any case, does a model with no group-level varying parameters contain any identifying information
about the covariance terms of the multivariate distribution/the scaling matrix `a` in Andrew's example above? 
To my mind, all the covariation for a single group's parameters will be captured in the joint posterior of the 
means (as we get when we use univariate priors), and we'd only be able to draw inference about the 
covariance matrix of a multivariate distribution if we have multiple groups. Is my intuition way off here?

Cheers, 
Jim

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] On using multivariate priors for non-varying parameters
parts:
Wasn't Andrew making the point the other week that if we scale covariates and then select a prior, 
the prior is actually conceived with knowledge of the data, and isn't really a prior? This is a part of 
my confusion. In any case, I think Andrew's point above is about scaling the parameters, not the 
covariates.

Yeah, there is a certain empirical Bayes feel here, but it’s subtle because the corrections
are done on the data and in some sense aren’t different from any of the other preprocesing/
cleaning that is done to measurements.  By the way, this is a really nice example of why
in practice it is nearly impossible to actually choose priors before seeing the data, and hence
why marginal likelihood-based techniques can be so fragile.

What would make sense to me is if using a multivariate prior helped old-school samplers better
explore the parameter space. 

In any case, does a model with no group-level varying parameters contain any identifying information
about the covariance terms of the multivariate distribution/the scaling matrix `a` in Andrew's example above? 
To my mind, all the covariation for a single group's parameters will be captured in the joint posterior of the 
means (as we get when we use univariate priors), and we'd only be able to draw inference about the 
covariance matrix of a multivariate distribution if we have multiple groups. Is my intuition way off here?

They are very much different models, and so they will have different performance.

Because we’re considering just the continuous covariate term, X * beta, there’s
always going to be some subtle ambiguity between covariance between the covariates
and the slopes.  For example, if we can implement a N(0, Sigma) prior on the beta as

X * L * beta_tilde,

where the beta_tilde are IID gaussians and L is the Cholesky decomposition of Sigma.

But we can achieve nearly the same model by instead taking

(X * L) * beta_tilde

which can be implemented by standardizing the data, or using the QR decomposition
a la rstanarm.  

Now these are technically different models, L is variable in the former and constant in
the latter, but they do achieve similar results of decorrelating the covariates and hence
making the model easier to fit.  Indeed, one could reasonable make the argument that
taking L from the empirical covariance of the data is an empirical Bayes approximation
to giving the beta a multivariate gaussian prior with unknown covariance that must be
learned from the data.
